items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A tiny negative particle that orbits the nucleus"?
items.answer: electron
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of electron.

items.stem: Aiko writes: "Molecules are always compounds." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Some molecules, such as O₂, H₂ and N₂, contain only one element and are elements.
items.markingKey: Some molecules, such as O₂, H₂ and N₂, contain only one element and are elements. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a molecule and an atom.
items.answer: An atom is a single particle of an element; a molecule is two or more atoms chemically bonded together (of the same or different elements).
items.markingKey: An atom is a single particle of an element; a molecule is two or more atoms chemically bonded together (of the same or different elements). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: In an investigation into how the number of atoms in a model molecule affects its mass, using modelling kits as a model of real molecules, explain why the same type of balls and connectors must be used in every trial.
items.answer: different kits have different masses
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a change in this variable (the same type of balls and connectors) would also affect the dependent variable; 1 mark for the specific reason: different kits have different masses. Then only the independent variable is responsible for any change (validity).

items.stem:
Freya measured the mass of different volumes of pure aluminium (an element) using a balance and a displacement can, three samples of each volume.

Volume / cm³ | Mass / g: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
2 | 4.7 | 5.0 | 5.0
4 | 9.7 | 9.7 | 9.9
6 | 9.4 | 14.1 | 14.1
8 | 20.1 | 19.0 | 19.7
10 | 24.6 | 24.9 | 24.5

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean mass at 6 cm³, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 9.4 g (trial 1 at 6 cm³); mean = 14.10 g
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (9.4) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 14.10 g.

items.stem: Briefly describe John Dalton’s atomic theory (1803) and explain what it reveals about development of atomic ideas.
items.answer: Dalton proposed that all matter is made of indivisible atoms, that atoms of one element are identical and that compounds form from atoms combining in fixed ratios. His model was later improved (atoms do contain smaller particles), showing how scientific models change with new evidence.
items.markingKey: Context (Dalton proposed that all matter is made of indivisible atoms, that atoms of one element are identical and that compounds form from atoms combining in fixed ratios.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: His model was later improved (atoms do contain smaller particles), showing how scientific models change with new evidence. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to development of atomic ideas.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Dalton’s solid-sphere model of the atom should no longer be taught because it is wrong."
items.answer: Simple models remain useful when their limitations are understood.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: we now know atoms contain protons, neutrons and electrons. Arguments against: still useful for explaining reactions and states of matter; shows how models develop. Supported judgement: Simple models remain useful when their limitations are understood.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the number of atoms in a model molecule affects its mass, using modelling kits as a model of real molecules. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Build models of CH₄ to C₆H₁₄ using one kit; zero the balance; weigh each model three times; calculate means; plot mass against number of carbon atoms; compare the pattern with real relative formula masses (16, 30, 44, …).
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (small parts – keep away from mouths; tidy up to avoid slips). Model: Build models of CH₄ to C₆H₁₄ using one kit; zero the balance; weigh each model three times; calculate means; plot mass against number of carbon atoms; compare the pattern with real relative formula masses (16, 30, 44, …).

items.stem: Explain why an element cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical reactions.
items.answer: It contains only one type of atom, so there is nothing simpler for it to break into chemically.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It contains only one type of atom, so there is nothing simpler for it to break into chemically. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a proton and an electron.
items.answer: A proton is positive with relative mass 1 and is in the nucleus; an electron is negative with tiny mass and orbits the nucleus.
items.markingKey: A proton is positive with relative mass 1 and is in the nucleus; an electron is negative with tiny mass and orbits the nucleus. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Elena is investigating how the number of atoms in a model molecule affects its mass, using modelling kits as a model of real molecules. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: number of carbon “atoms” (balls) in a model hydrocarbon chain (1 to 6)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: number of carbon “atoms” (balls) in a model hydrocarbon chain (1 to 6) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: Describe the structure of an atom and explain how the particles in it differ in charge, mass and position.
items.answer: Tiny central nucleus containing protons (+1, mass 1) and neutrons (0, mass 1); electrons (−1, very small mass ≈ 1/1840) in shells around the nucleus; atom has equal protons and electrons so is neutral; most of the atom is empty space; number of protons identifies the element.
items.markingKey: Tiny central nucleus containing protons (+1, mass 1) and neutrons (0, mass 1); electrons (−1, very small mass ≈ 1/1840) in shells around the nucleus; atom has equal protons and electrons so is neutral; most of the atom is empty space; number of protons identifies the element.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "period"?
options: A one- or two-letter code for an element, e.g. Na for sodium
Symbols and numbers showing the elements and number of atoms in a substance, e.g. H₂O
An equation showing the names of the reactants and products in a reaction
A horizontal row of the periodic table
items.answer: A horizontal row of the periodic table
items.markingKey: D. "period" is a horizontal row of the periodic table.

items.stem: Explain why helium is used in balloons instead of hydrogen.
items.answer: Both are less dense than air, but helium is unreactive (a noble gas) so it does not burn or explode.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Both are less dense than air, but helium is unreactive (a noble gas) so it does not burn or explode. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a period and a group.
items.answer: A group is a vertical column of elements with similar properties; a period is a horizontal row across the table.
items.markingKey: A group is a vertical column of elements with similar properties; a period is a horizontal row across the table. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which Mendeleev and gallium (1869–1875) shows prediction in science.
items.answer: Mendeleev predicted “eka-aluminium” with density about 5.9 g/cm³; gallium was discovered in 1875 with density 5.9 g/cm³. Correct predictions convinced scientists that his periodic table was a powerful scientific model.
items.markingKey: Context (Mendeleev predicted “eka-aluminium” with density about 5.9 g/cm³; gallium was discovered in 1875 with density 5.9 g/cm³.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Correct predictions convinced scientists that his periodic table was a powerful scientific model. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to prediction in science.

items.stem: "Elements are arranged in order of their mass." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The modern periodic table is arranged by atomic number (number of protons).
items.markingKey: The modern periodic table is arranged by atomic number (number of protons). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how well different elements conduct electricity. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): iodine is harmful – handle in a sealed tube; do not touch hot wires. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. iodine is harmful – handle in a sealed tube; do not touch hot wires); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A vertical column of the periodic table containing elements with similar properties"?
items.answer: group
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of group.

items.stem: An element is described as: black solid that conducts electricity but is brittle and not shiny. Is it most likely a metal or a non-metal?
items.answer: non-metal
items.markingKey: B. B1 non-metal (graphite is an exception)

items.stem:
Tomás heated one end of a copper rod in a water bath at 80 °C and measured the temperature rise at the other end over time (three rods).

Time / min | Temperature rise / °C: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 6.7 | 6.2 | 6.3
2 | 11.1 | 11.6 | 11.5
4 | 12.1 | 18.3 | 18.0
6 | 23.3 | 22.9 | 22.1
8 | 25.0 | 25.2 | 25.8

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean temperature rise at 4 min, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 12.1 °C (trial 1 at 4 min); mean = 18.15 °C
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (12.1) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 18.15 °C.

items.stem: How many atoms are in one molecule of H₂O?
items.markingKey: 3. Two H and one O.

items.stem: Explain why a compound always has the same formula.
items.answer: Elements combine in fixed proportions; e.g. water always has two hydrogen atoms for every oxygen atom.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Elements combine in fixed proportions; e.g. water always has two hydrogen atoms for every oxygen atom. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Iron sulfide is just iron and sulfur mixed together." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Iron sulfide is a compound; the iron and sulfur are chemically bonded and it is not magnetic, unlike a mixture of iron and sulfur.
items.markingKey: Iron sulfide is a compound; the iron and sulfur are chemically bonded and it is not magnetic, unlike a mixture of iron and sulfur. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Lukas plans to investigate how the mass of magnesium burned affects the mass of magnesium oxide formed. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: heating until no further change; lid lifted only slightly; the same crucible; crucible cooled before weighing
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: heating until no further change – all magnesium must react; lid lifted only slightly – prevents smoke (oxide) escaping; the same crucible – crucibles differ in mass; crucible cooled before weighing – hot objects give inaccurate readings. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem:
Isabel heated different masses of copper powder in air until there was no further change and recorded the mass of copper oxide formed.

Mass of copper / g | Mass of copper oxide / g: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.5 | 0.59 | 0.59 | 0.57
1.0 | 1.14 | 1.21 | 1.19
1.5 | 1.77 | 1.71 | 1.83
2.0 | 2.40 | 2.36 | 2.32
2.5 | 2.84 | 2.85 | 2.86

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The mass of copper oxide is directly proportional to the mass of copper. Copper and oxygen combine in a fixed ratio to form the compound copper oxide, so doubling the copper doubles the oxide formed.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The mass of copper oxide is directly proportional to the mass of copper.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Copper and oxygen combine in a fixed ratio to form the compound copper oxide, so doubling the copper doubles the oxide formed.

items.stem: The formula of calcium carbonate is CaCO₃. State the number of each type of atom in one unit of CaCO₃ and the total number of atoms.
items.answer: 1 Ca, 1 C, 3 O; total 5 atoms
items.markingKey: 1 correct number of each element (1 Ca, 1 C, 3 O); 1 total 5.

items.stem: Iron and sulfur are heated together. Compare the mixture before heating with the product after heating, describing two tests and naming the product.
items.answer: Before: grey iron filings and yellow sulfur visible; a magnet separates the iron; sulfur dissolves in some solvents. After heating: glows, black solid iron sulfide (a compound) forms; not attracted to magnet; fixed composition FeS; new properties. Word equation: iron + sulfur → iron sulfide.
items.markingKey: Before: grey iron filings and yellow sulfur visible; a magnet separates the iron; sulfur dissolves in some solvents. After heating: glows, black solid iron sulfide (a compound) forms; not attracted to magnet; fixed composition FeS; new properties. Word equation: iron + sulfur → iron sulfide.

items.stem: Omar investigated how the mass of magnesium burned affects the mass of magnesium oxide formed. The method had this weakness: white smoke escaped when the lid was lifted. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: lift the lid only slightly and briefly with tongs
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: lift the lid only slightly and briefly with tongs

items.stem: Briefly explain why the properties of a compound are different from the elements it is made from.
items.answer: The atoms are chemically bonded into a new substance with a new arrangement, so it has new properties – e.g. sodium (reactive metal) and chlorine (toxic gas) form salt.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The atoms are chemically bonded into a new substance with a new arrangement, so it has new properties – e.g. sodium (reactive metal) and chlorine (toxic gas) form salt. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a compound and an element.
items.answer: An element contains only one type of atom; a compound contains two or more different elements chemically bonded in fixed proportions.
items.markingKey: An element contains only one type of atom; a compound contains two or more different elements chemically bonded in fixed proportions. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Omar heated different masses of copper powder in air until there was no further change and recorded the mass of copper oxide formed.

Mass of copper / g | Mass of copper oxide / g: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.5 | 0.60 | 0.59 | 0.59
1.0 | 1.14 | 1.16 | 0.75
1.5 | 1.81 | 1.76 | 1.77
2.0 | 2.37 | 2.26 | 2.31
2.5 | 2.89 | 3.01 | 2.84

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean mass of copper oxide at 1.0 g, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 0.75 g (trial 3 at 1.0 g); mean = 1.15 g
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (0.75) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 1.15 g.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "crystallisation".
items.answer: Obtaining a soluble solid from a solution by evaporating some solvent and leaving it to form crystals
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: obtaining a soluble solid from a solution by evaporating some solvent and leaving it to form crystals. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a condenser is cooled with cold water in distillation.
items.answer: The cold water cools the vapour so it condenses back into liquid that can be collected.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The cold water cools the vapour so it condenses back into liquid that can be collected. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between simple distillation and fractional distillation.
items.answer: Simple distillation separates a solvent from a solution; fractional distillation separates liquids with similar boiling points using a fractionating column.
items.markingKey: Simple distillation separates a solvent from a solution; fractional distillation separates liquids with similar boiling points using a fractionating column. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: In an investigation into how the type of solvent affects how far the dyes in a felt-tip pen travel in chromatography, state the dependent variable and describe how Isabel should measure it.
items.answer: Rf value of each dye spot
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: Rf value of each dye spot.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Desalination in the Middle East shows separation on a large scale.
items.answer: Countries such as Saudi Arabia and the UAE get much of their drinking water by distilling or using reverse osmosis on sea water. It provides water in deserts but uses large amounts of energy and returns very salty brine to the sea.
items.markingKey: Context (Countries such as Saudi Arabia and the UAE get much of their drinking water by distilling or using reverse osmosis on sea water.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It provides water in deserts but uses large amounts of energy and returns very salty brine to the sea. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to separation on a large scale.

items.stem: Plan how to obtain pure, dry salt crystals from a mixture of rock salt (salt, sand and grit). Explain each step.
items.answer: Grind with pestle and mortar (more surface); add warm water and stir (salt dissolves, sand doesn’t); filter (sand stays as residue, salt solution is filtrate); heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin until crystals start to form; leave to cool and crystallise; pat dry with filter paper or warm oven.
items.markingKey: Grind with pestle and mortar (more surface); add warm water and stir (salt dissolves, sand doesn’t); filter (sand stays as residue, salt solution is filtrate); heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin until crystals start to form; leave to cool and crystallise; pat dry with filter paper or warm oven.

items.stem: Which method separates the dyes in black ink?
items.answer: Paper chromatography
items.markingKey: D. Dyes move different distances.

items.markingKey: M1 (4.8 + 5.0 + 4.8) ÷ 3; A1 4.87 g (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Desalination is the best solution to water shortages."
items.answer: Desalination is valuable in very dry coastal regions but should be combined with saving water and renewable energy.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: unlimited sea water; reliable supply in dry regions. Arguments against: very high energy use and cost; brine harms marine life; saving water and fixing leaks is cheaper. Supported judgement: Desalination is valuable in very dry coastal regions but should be combined with saving water and renewable energy. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: What happens to the mass when 5 g of sugar dissolves in 100 g of water?
items.answer: The solution has a mass of 105 g
items.markingKey: The solution has a mass of 105 g. Mass is conserved.

items.stem: Explain the difference between melting and dissolving.
items.answer: Dissolving is a solute spreading out in a solvent to form a solution; melting is a solid turning into a liquid by heating.
items.markingKey: Dissolving is a solute spreading out in a solvent to form a solution; melting is a solid turning into a liquid by heating. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why fizzy drinks go flat faster when warm.
items.answer: Carbon dioxide is less soluble in warmer water, so it comes out of solution as bubbles more quickly. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Carbon dioxide is less soluble in warmer water, so it comes out of solution as bubbles more quickly. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Mohammed plans to investigate how the temperature of water affects the mass of potassium nitrate that dissolves in it. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: mass of water (10 g); stirring for the same time; adding in 0.5 g portions; the same batch of potassium nitrate
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: mass of water (10 g) – more water dissolves more; stirring for the same time – ensures the solution is saturated; adding in 0.5 g portions – affects the precision of the result; the same batch of potassium nitrate – purity affects results. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem:
Noah measured the mass of a salt that dissolved in 100 g of water at different temperatures.

30 | 52 | 52 | 52

items.answer: 50 °C; range = 6 g/100 g water; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Water is the most important solvent on Earth."
items.answer: Water is the most important solvent for life, though other solvents are essential in industry.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: dissolves many substances, transporting nutrients in organisms and soils; life’s reactions take place in water. Arguments against: many industrial and cleaning processes need other solvents (e.g. ethanol for perfumes). Supported judgement: Water is the most important solvent for life, though other solvents are essential in industry.

items.stem: In salt water, what is the solvent?
items.answer: Water
items.markingKey: D. The solute is salt.

items.stem: Rafael writes: "Water can dissolve everything." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Many substances, such as sand, oil and plastics, are insoluble in water but may dissolve in other solvents.
items.markingKey: Many substances, such as sand, oil and plastics, are insoluble in water but may dissolve in other solvents. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Tomás investigated how the temperature of water affects the mass of potassium nitrate that dissolves in it. The method had this weakness: the solution cooled while solid was being added. items.answer: keep the tube in the water bath throughout and check the temperature

items.stem: What is the chemical symbol for sodium?
items.answer: Na

items.stem: What is the name of the compound formed when magnesium burns in oxygen?
items.answer: Magnesium oxide

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "malleable".
items.answer: Can be hammered into shape without breaking

items.answer: A dilute solution has a small amount of solute in the solvent; a concentrated solution has a large amount of solute in the same volume.

items.answer: Some molecules, such as O₂, H₂ and N₂, contain only one element and are elements.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Using chemical names is better than common names (like “salt” or “baking soda”) on food labels."
items.answer: Labels should give both: the chemical name for precision and the common name for understanding.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: precise, avoids confusion; helps people with allergies. Arguments against: many people do not understand chemical names; can make safe foods sound frightening. Supported judgement: Labels should give both: the chemical name for precision and the common name for understanding.

items.stem: An unknown element is a shiny solid that conducts electricity and can be bent without breaking. Classify it, predict where it is in the periodic table and describe two other properties you would expect it to have.
items.answer: It is a metal (shiny, conductor, malleable); found on the left or in the centre of the periodic table; expected: good thermal conductor, high melting point and density, forms basic oxides, sonorous, possibly reacts with acids to give hydrogen.
items.markingKey: It is a metal (shiny, conductor, malleable); found on the left or in the centre of the periodic table; expected: good thermal conductor, high melting point and density, forms basic oxides, sonorous, possibly reacts with acids to give hydrogen.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the type of solvent affects how far the dyes in a felt-tip pen travel in chromatography. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Draw a pencil line 2 cm from the bottom of four strips; add a small spot of ink; stand each strip in a different solvent below the line with a lid on; remove when the solvent is 1 cm from the top; mark the solvent front; measure distances and calculate Rf values; repeat twice.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (ethanol and propanone are flammable – no flames; use in a well-ventilated room). Model: Draw a pencil line 2 cm from the bottom of four strips; add a small spot of ink; stand each strip in a different solvent below the line with a lid on; remove when the solvent is 1 cm from the top; mark the solvent front; measure distances and calculate Rf values; repeat twice.

items.stem: Use particle ideas to explain what a saturated solution is, and describe how to make a saturated solution of potassium nitrate at 40 °C and find its solubility.
items.answer: Saturated: no more solute can dissolve – solvent particles cannot surround any more solute particles at that temperature. Method: heat 50 g water to 40 °C in a water bath; add weighed potassium nitrate in small portions stirring until some remains undissolved; filter warm; weigh an evaporating basin, add a known mass of the solution, evaporate to dryness, weigh the solid; solubility = mass of solid ÷ mass of water × 100 g.
items.markingKey: Saturated: no more solute can dissolve – solvent particles cannot surround any more solute particles at that temperature. Method: heat 50 g water to 40 °C in a water bath; add weighed potassium nitrate in small portions stirring until some remains undissolved; filter warm; weigh an evaporating basin, add a known mass of the solution, evaporate to dryness, weigh the solid; solubility = mass of solid ÷ mass of water × 100 g.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "element".
items.answer: A substance made of only one type of atom
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a substance made of only one type of atom. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A new substance made in a chemical reaction"?
items.answer: product
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of product.

items.stem: Which property is typical of non-metals?
items.answer: Poor conductor of electricity
items.markingKey: Poor conductor of electricity. Except graphite.

items.stem: A student claims: "Filtration can remove salt from sea water." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Salt is dissolved; dissolved particles pass through filter paper. Distillation is needed.
items.markingKey: Salt is dissolved; dissolved particles pass through filter paper. Distillation is needed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why crushed sugar dissolves faster than a sugar cube.
items.answer: Crushing increases the surface area in contact with the water, so more particles can be pulled into solution each second.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Crushing increases the surface area in contact with the water, so more particles can be pulled into solution each second. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why chemical symbols are useful to scientists around the world.
items.answer: They are the same in every language, so scientists can communicate clearly and write formulae and equations.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They are the same in every language, so scientists can communicate clearly and write formulae and equations. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Sofia writes: "The small number in H₂O means there are two water molecules." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The subscript 2 applies to hydrogen: each molecule contains 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom.
items.markingKey: The subscript 2 applies to hydrogen: each molecule contains 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "All metals are solid and magnetic." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Mercury is a liquid, and only iron, nickel and cobalt (and some alloys) are magnetic.
items.markingKey: Mercury is a liquid, and only iron, nickel and cobalt (and some alloys) are magnetic. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why a mixture of salt and sand can be separated by adding water, filtering and evaporating.
items.answer: Salt dissolves in water but sand does not; filtration removes the sand; evaporating the filtrate leaves salt crystals.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Salt dissolves in water but sand does not; filtration removes the sand; evaporating the filtrate leaves salt crystals. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Mei measured the mass of a salt that dissolved in 100 g of water at different temperatures.

Temperature / °C | Solubility / g/100 g water: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
10 | 31 | 32 | 31
20 | 44 | 45 | 45
30 | 62 | 63 | 62
40 | 89 | 85 | 89
50 | 117 | 114 | 109

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The solubility increases as temperature increases, and increases more steeply at higher temperatures. At higher temperatures water particles have more kinetic energy and can separate and surround more solute particles.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The solubility increases as temperature increases, and increases more steeply at higher temperatures.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: At higher temperatures water particles have more kinetic energy and can separate and surround more solute particles.

items.stem: With reference to John Dalton’s atomic theory (1803), explain how it illustrates development of atomic ideas.
items.answer: Dalton proposed that all matter is made of indivisible atoms, that atoms of one element are identical and that compounds form from atoms combining in fixed ratios. His model was later improved (atoms do contain smaller particles), showing how scientific models change with new evidence.

items.stem: The formula of sodium hydroxide is NaOH. State the number of each type of atom in one unit of NaOH and the total number of atoms.
items.answer: 1 Na, 1 O, 1 H; total 3 atoms
items.markingKey: 1 correct number of each element (1 Na, 1 O, 1 H); 1 total 3.

items.stem: With reference to Mendeleev and gallium (1869–1875), explain how it illustrates prediction in science.
items.answer: Mendeleev predicted “eka-aluminium” with density about 5.9 g/cm³; gallium was discovered in 1875 with density 5.9 g/cm³. Correct predictions convinced scientists that his periodic table was a powerful scientific model.
items.markingKey: Context (Mendeleev predicted “eka-aluminium” with density about 5.9 g/cm³; gallium was discovered in 1875 with density 5.9 g/cm³.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: A blue food dye has an Rf value of 0.6. If the solvent front moves 6 cm, how far would the dye move?
items.answer: 3.6 cm
items.markingKey: M1 distance = Rf × solvent distance = 0.6 × 6; A1 3.6 cm.

items.stem: A student claims: "Water can dissolve everything." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Many substances, such as sand, oil and plastics, are insoluble in water but may dissolve in other solvents.
items.markingKey: Many substances, such as sand, oil and plastics, are insoluble in water but may dissolve in other solvents. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Isabel measured the mass of different volumes of pure aluminium (an element) using a balance and a displacement can, three samples of each volume.

Volume / cm³ | Mass / g: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
2 | 5.4 | 5.0 | 5.4
4 | 10.1 | 10.5 | 10.4
6 | 16.0 | 15.9 | 16.0
8 | 20.3 | 20.3 | 20.3
10 | 24.9 | 26.6 | 26.6

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The mass increases in direct proportion to the volume of aluminium. An element contains only one type of atom; every aluminium atom has the same mass and the atoms are packed the same way, so doubling the volume doubles the number of atoms and the mass.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The mass increases in direct proportion to the volume of aluminium.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: An element contains only one type of atom; every aluminium atom has the same mass and the atoms are packed the same way, so doubling the volume doubles the number of atoms and the mass.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the mass of magnesium burned affects the mass of magnesium oxide formed. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Weigh a crucible and lid; add coiled magnesium and reweigh; heat strongly, lifting the lid occasionally to let oxygen in; when no more glowing, heat for 2 more minutes; cool and reweigh; calculate oxide mass; repeat for each mass and plot mass of oxide against mass of magnesium.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (do not look directly at burning magnesium; use tongs, a heatproof mat and eye protection; the crucible stays hot for a long time). Model: Weigh a crucible and lid; add coiled magnesium and reweigh; heat strongly, lifting the lid occasionally to let oxygen in; when no more glowing, heat for 2 more minutes; cool and reweigh; calculate oxide mass; repeat for each mass and plot mass of oxide against mass of magnesium.

items.stem: "Rare metals used in phones should be recycled by law." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Recycling laws are justified because supplies are limited and mining causes harm, even if costs are high.

items.stem: "Desalination is the best solution to water shortages." Discuss.
items.answer: Desalination is valuable in very dry coastal regions but should be combined with saving water and renewable energy.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the temperature of water affects the mass of potassium nitrate that dissolves in it. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Put 10 g water in a boiling tube in a water bath at 20 °C; add 0.5 g portions of potassium nitrate, stirring for 1 min each, until some stays undissolved; record the total mass dissolved; repeat at each temperature; repeat three times; calculate solubility per 100 g water and plot a solubility curve.
